lesson_title: The Graph That Lies: Reading Data Displays
hook_text: "Winter electricity use QUADRUPLES." It went up 14 percent. Here's exactly how the picture lied.
clip_script: A family buys prepaid electricity. May: 420 units. June: 480 units. Now a newspaper draws those two as bars — but starts the bottom of the axis at 400 instead of zero. Watch what happens. May has 20 units sticking up above the line. June has 80. Four times as tall. Headline: electricity use quadruples. It did not. It went up 60 units on 420 — that's about 14 out of every 100, roughly 14 percent. The numbers never lied. The picture did, by cutting the bottom off the axis. And once you know the trick you'll see it everywhere. A pie chart tilted in three dimensions makes the front slice look fatter than an equal slice at the back. A little picture drawn twice as tall AND twice as wide looks four times as big — but only stands for double. So before you believe any graph: where does the scale start, are the gaps even, is every axis labelled, and is the total actually given? Make your eyes wait for the numbers.
visual_style: Two bars on a clean axis; the axis baseline slides up from 0 to 400 and the bars stretch grotesquely, then snap back as the true 14 percent gap appears; quick beats of a tilted pie and a doubling pictogram.
mood: Sharp, slightly conspiratorial — the pleasure of catching someone out.
pacing: Slow reveal on the sliding axis, rapid-fire on the other tricks, firm four-question close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never be fooled by a picture of numbers again.
